enthusiastic

/en-THOO-zee-as-tik/ — emphasis on THOO · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Someone who is enthusiastic shows strong excitement and eager interest in something.

The enthusiastic crowd cheered every point, even in the rain.

Example

When the coach announced the training program, every player was enthusiastic — nodding, asking detailed questions, and volunteering for extra drills.

Enthusiastic is precise here because it captures both the eager interest in the activity and the active, visible excitement. Interested would miss how openly they show their eagerness and willingness through their actions.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

keen: Keen means eagerly interested and ready to act, and that eagerness can stay entirely quiet — a keen reader just keeps reading. Enthusiastic adds open, visible excitement: hands shooting up, questions asked, extra work volunteered for. Keen is the appetite itself; enthusiastic is the appetite on full display.

passionate: Passionate means driven by strong, heartfelt emotion — the feeling runs deep and personal, and it can be solemn rather than upbeat. Enthusiastic is lighter and more outward: bright, eager excitement you can watch in someone's actions. You can be quietly passionate about justice; an enthusiastic fan is visibly buzzing.

ardent: Ardent means burning with warm, devoted eagerness, usually fixed on one beloved cause or person, and the devotion lasts. Enthusiastic is broader and more everyday: openly excited and eager about an activity, no vow of loyalty required. An ardent supporter is devoted for years; an enthusiastic one is eager today.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

apathetic: showing no interest, energy, or concern

halfhearted: done without real effort or enthusiasm

Where it sits · how eagerly someone throws themselves in

indifferent → interested → excited → enthusiastic

indifferent vs. enthusiastic: Indifferent is the opposite of enthusiastic: an indifferent person shrugs and simply doesn't care, while an enthusiastic one can hardly wait to join in.

interested vs. enthusiastic: Interested is much weaker than enthusiastic — an interested student listens attentively, while an enthusiastic one volunteers, asks questions, and begs for more.

excited vs. enthusiastic: Excited is strong, but enthusiastic adds eager commitment: excitement is the buzz of a single moment, while an enthusiastic person keeps that energy going project after project.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — en-: in, within (Greek)

Root — thusi: god (from Greek theos, 'god'; spelled -thusi- inside this word)

Suffix — -ast: one who (Greek agent ending, as in enthusiast or gymnast)

Suffix — -ic: characteristic of (Greek)

Put it together: En- ('in, within') + thusi ('god,' from Greek theos) + -ast ('one who') + -ic ('characteristic of') — to the ancient Greeks an enthusiastic person had 'a god within,' possessed by divine inspiration. Today it means filled with that same fired-up, eager energy.

Use the root in a new word: theology: Theology, the study of God, uses the same Greek root theos that gives enthusiastic its original meaning of having 'a god within.'

Word Building

Word Choice

neutral

Enthusiastic describes someone who shows both excitement and eager interest through their actions and words. Use it when someone actively demonstrates their eagerness—raising their hand in class, volunteering, asking questions, participating fully. For someone who's merely willing or interested, the simpler words 'interested' or 'willing' are usually better.
